bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `pipeline(x, fns)`: pass `x` through each function in the array, in order, and return the final value. Empty array → `x` unchanged.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: This is composition applied immediately: output feeds the next input until the list is exhausted. The empty-list case returning x unchanged shows identity is the natural "zero" of composition.
hints: A loop reassigning one value variable — or reduce.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `pipe(...fns)` returning ONE function that applies every fn left to right. `pipe()` with no functions returns the identity function.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: reduce’s accumulator plays the role of "the value so far", seeded with the input; each function replaces it. With no functions, reduce returns the seed untouched — identity for free, no special case needed.
hints: Rest-collect the fns; the returned function reduces over them with x as the seed.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `compose(...fns)` returning one function that applies fns RIGHT to LEFT: `compose(f, g, h)(x)` = `f(g(h(x)))`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: reduceRight walks the array from the end, so the LAST listed function touches x first — exactly the mathematical convention. pipe and compose differ by one word; pick per readability and stay consistent.
hints: Same as pipe but with reduceRight.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `applyN(fn, n, x)` that applies `fn` to `x` a total of `n` times: `applyN(f, 3, x)` = `f(f(f(x)))`. `n = 0` returns `x`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Composing a function with ITSELF n times is iteration expressed as composition. applyN(f, 0, x) = x again shows identity as composition’s zero — the same value pipe() returned.
hints: pipeline(x, [fn, fn, fn]) — but with a counted loop.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `negate(pred)` returning a new predicate that is `true` exactly when `pred(x)` is falsy.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: negate composes a boolean NOT onto any predicate, so you define isEven once and derive isOdd. This is how myReject related to myFilter — now expressed as a reusable transformer.
hints: Wrap the call in ! inside a new arrow.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `allPass(preds)` (array of predicates) returning one predicate that is `true` when EVERY pred passes. Empty array → always `true`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: allPass combines predicates with logical AND, producing a single function filter can use. Validation rule lists become one gate: `rows.filter(allPass(rules))`.
hints: The returned predicate calls every() over the array with x.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `anyPass(preds)` returning one predicate that is `true` when AT LEAST ONE pred passes. Empty array → always `false`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: The OR-combinator mirrors allPass exactly — every/some are the duals from the callbacks lesson resurfacing at the combinator level. Empty-case conventions (true for AND, false for OR) follow the identity of each boolean operation.
hints: some() instead of every().

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `mapPipe(arr, fns)`: return a new array where each element has been passed through every function in `fns`, in order.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Two higher-order tools nested: map supplies each element, and the inner reduce runs the pipeline on it. Equivalent to arr.map(pipe(...fns)) — composition lets the two spellings coexist.
hints: map outside, reduce (the pipeline) inside.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `sanitize(s)` that trims, lowercases, and collapses every run of spaces to a single '-': `sanitize('  Hello   World  ')` → `'hello-world'`. Build it from small steps (the tests only check behavior).
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Each step is a one-liner you could test alone; the export just names their composition. Splitting on /\s+/ handles runs of spaces that a replaceAll of single spaces would turn into repeated dashes — the step boundaries make such fixes local.
hints: trim first (so outer spaces don’t become dashes), then lowercase, then split on whitespace runs and join with -.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `withDefault(fn, fallback)` returning a new function: it calls `fn(x)` and returns the result, unless that result is `null` or `undefined`, in which case it returns `fallback`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: withDefault composes a nullish-guard onto any function, the same way negate composed a NOT onto predicates. Using `??` (not `||`) keeps legitimate falsy results like 0 and "" — the distinction firstResult made manually, now packaged as a reusable combinator.
hints: The ?? operator replaces only null/undefined — exactly the contract.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions:
Export `finalPrice(cents, discountPct, taxRate)`: apply the discount first (round with Math.round), then add tax on the discounted price (round the tax too). Build each step as its own small function.
Example: finalPrice(1000, 10, 0.08) → discounted 900 → tax 72 → 972.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Factories configure the steps, composition fixes their order — the two patterns of this course working together. The order is not stylistic: taxing before discounting gives a different (wrong) number, and the pipeline documents the chosen rule at a glance.
hints: Two factory-built steps (factories lesson!) composed in order.
Order is business logic: tax applies to the DISCOUNTED price.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions:
Export `createTransformer(steps)` where `steps` is an array of step NAMES from this registry:
- `'trim'` — s.trim()
- `'lower'` — s.toLowerCase()
- `'upper'` — s.toUpperCase()
- `'exclaim'` — s + '!'
- `'snake'` — replace every space with '_'
Return a function applying the named steps to a string in order. If any name is unknown, `createTransformer` itself must throw `new Error('unknown step: ' + name)` immediately (before the returned function is ever called).
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Names (data) are resolved through a dispatch table into functions (behavior), validated eagerly, then composed — this one exercise joins dispatch tables, factories, and pipe. Failing at creation time, not call time, is a real API-design principle: configuration errors should surface where the configuration is written. This is how template engines, middleware stacks, and build pipelines are configured from JSON.
hints: Map the names to functions through a registry object (dispatch table!).
Validate during the map — throwing early beats failing on first use.
The returned function is just pipe over the resolved fns.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: In an object literal, `inc() { ... }` is shorthand for which of these?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Method shorthand creates a REGULAR function property — crucially not an arrow. That means it gets a real `this` from the call site, which is what a method needs.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: When you call `user.getName()`, what is `this` inside `getName`?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: For regular functions, the call-site rule is: the receiver (the value before the dot) becomes `this`. Same function, different receiver → different `this`. The dot is doing the work.

Extracting the method into `f` keeps the function but loses the receiver. A plain `f()` call in strict mode (all modules) sets `this` to undefined, and reading `.name` off undefined throws. This is THE classic `this` bug.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Why is `greet: () => "Hi " + this.name` broken inside an object literal?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: An object literal does not create a scope; the arrow inherits `this` from the enclosing module/function, which has nothing to do with the object it happens to sit in. Methods that use `this` must be regular functions.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Which fixes the lost-`this` bug when passing `obj.method` as a callback?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: bind pre-attaches the receiver; the arrow wrapper re-creates the dot call every time. Both preserve `this`. Option 3 CALLS the method immediately and passes its result — a different bug from the first lesson.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: What does `greet.call(otherUser)` do, where `greet` is a regular function using `this.name`?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: `call` invokes a function once with an explicit `this` (and arguments after it). Unlike `bind`, it does not create a new function — it is a one-shot receiver override, useful for borrowing methods.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Inside a method `start() { setTimeout(() => this.tick(), 100); }` — why is the ARROW the right choice for the callback?
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: setTimeout invokes its callback as a plain call, so a regular function would receive `this = undefined`. The arrow has no own `this` and transparently uses the enclosing method’s — which is the object, because start() was called with a dot. Methods regular, callbacks arrow.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Each `counter.inc()` call binds `this` to `counter`, so the method mutates the object’s own `count` property: 1, then 2, and reading `counter.count` directly confirms the state lives on the object (unlike a closure, it is publicly visible).

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Called as obj.regular(), the regular method gets `this = obj` → 'object'. The arrow ignores the call site and inherits the module's top-level `this`, which is undefined in ES modules → 'undefined'. Same object, same dot-call, different `this` rules.
hints: In an ES module, top-level `this` is undefined. Which function inherits that?

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: bound() works — bind baked the receiver in, so this.name is 'Ada'. loose() is a plain call: this is undefined (strict mode), and undefined.name throws a TypeError, which the try/catch reports. Extract-then-call is exactly how methods get passed to event handlers and break.
hints: Modules run in strict mode: a plain call gets this = undefined.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `makeCounterObj()` returning `{ count: 0, inc(), reset() }`: `inc()` adds 1 to `this.count` and returns it; `reset()` sets it back to 0 and returns it. Use `this` (not a closure variable).
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Unlike the closure counter, the state is a public property and the methods reach it through `this` — the object-oriented spelling of the same idea. Which to use is a design choice: closures hide state, `this` exposes it.
hints: Method shorthand; both methods read/write this.count.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `makePlaylist()` returning `{ songs: [], add(song), size() }`: `add` pushes and returns `this` (so calls can chain); `size` returns the number of songs.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Returning `this` from a mutator is what makes fluent chains work: each `.add()` evaluates back to the playlist, so the next `.add()` has a receiver. jQuery, query builders, and test matchers all chain this way.
hints: return this at the end of add enables p.add(x).add(y).

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions:
Export `makeAccount(balance)` returning an object with a `balance` property and methods:
- `deposit(n)` — adds n, returns the new balance
- `withdraw(n)` — if n > balance return `'insufficient'` (unchanged); else subtract and return the new balance
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: The guard-before-mutate shape in withdraw keeps the object in a valid state — methods are where invariants live. `balance,` uses property shorthand to copy the parameter onto the object.
hints: The shorthand property `balance,` seeds the state; methods guard then mutate this.balance.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `makeRect(width, height)` returning `{ width, height, area(), scale(factor) }` where `area()` returns width × height and `scale(f)` multiplies BOTH dimensions by `f` and returns `this` for chaining.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: The chain `makeRect(2,3).scale(2).area()` only works because scale returns the mutated receiver — the test would get `undefined.area()` otherwise. Query/transform methods return values; fluent mutators return `this`.
hints: scale touches this.width and this.height, then returns this.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `makeLogger(prefix)` returning `{ prefix, lines: [], log(msg), output() }`: `log` pushes `this.prefix + ': ' + msg` onto `this.lines` and returns `this`; `output()` returns the lines joined with `'\n'`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Because the prefix is a property read through `this` on every call, changing `l.prefix` changes future lines — behavior a closure-captured prefix could never have. Property state is mutable and public; closure state is fixed at capture unless you expose mutators. Pick deliberately.
hints: log reads this.prefix at CALL time — a property, not a captured constant.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions:
Export `makeTodoList()` returning `{ todos: [], add(text), complete(text), pending() }`:
- `add(text)` pushes `{ text, done: false }`, returns `this`
- `complete(text)` sets `done: true` on the matching todo (if any), returns `this`
- `pending()` returns an array of the texts of not-done todos
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: Methods combine the array callbacks you built earlier (find, filter, map) with `this`-held state. Mutating the found todo is fine HERE because the object owns its own state — contrast with the pure-functions lesson, where the data belonged to the caller.
hints: find + mutate for complete; filter + map for pending.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: This `makeUser` is broken — calling `greet()` throws because the arrow function’s `this` is not the object. Fix `greet` so it works (keep using `this`).
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: The arrow captured the module’s top-level `this` (undefined in ESM), so `this.name` threw. Method shorthand creates a regular function whose `this` is supplied by `u.greet()` at each call — which is also why the second test passes after reassigning the property. Rule of thumb: methods shorthand, callbacks arrow.
hints: Arrows inherit this from where they are WRITTEN — here, the module (undefined).
Convert to method shorthand: greet() { ... } — a regular function that receives this from the dot-call.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions: Export `getBoundGreeter(user)`: `user` has a `greet()` method that uses `this`. Return a standalone function that can be called with NO receiver (e.g. passed as a callback) and still greets as `user`.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: bind solves the extraction problem by baking the receiver into a new function object — however it is later called, `this` is already decided. The arrow-wrapper alternative keeps the dot-call alive instead. Every "why is this undefined in my event handler" bug ends with one of these two fixes.
hints: user.greet alone would lose this the moment it is called plainly.
.bind(user) returns a NEW function with this permanently attached. An arrow wrapper () => user.greet() also works.

bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.instructions:
Export `makeCalc(start)` returning an object with methods `add(n)`, `sub(n)`, `mul(n)` — each updates an internal `value` and returns `this` — plus `result()` returning the current value.
`makeCalc(10).add(5).mul(2).sub(8).result()` → 22.
bootforge/functions-deep/applied-pattern.explanation: A fluent API in miniature: mutators return `this` so the chain keeps its receiver, and one terminal method (result) exits the chain with a value. The factory wrapper gives each calculator independent state — `this` for the methods, a fresh object per call for isolation. This is the exact architecture of expect(...).toBe chains and query builders.
hints: Every mutator ends with return this; only result() returns a number.
The chain works because each method call evaluates to the object itself.
